claim: VAPA KO cells exhibit a complete and specific depletion of VAPA protein.
source: VAPA KO cells exhibited a complete and specific depletion of VAPA protein (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A and B

claim: In VAPA KO cells, VAPB was well distributed throughout the ER and its levels were slightly increased, albeit non significant.
source: In VAPA KO cells, VAPB was well distributed throughout the ER and its levels were slightly increased, albeit non significant (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence and Western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: VAPA KO monolayers filled the open space less efficiently than Control monolayers in collective migration assays.
source: In these conditions, VAPA KO monolayers filled the open space less efficiently than Control monolayers (Figure 1D and E, Video 1).
evidence: Supported by phase contrast imaging and quantification of colonized surface shown in Figure 1D and E

claim: VAPA KO leader cells were displacing faster but with a remarkable lack of directionality compared to Control leader cells.
source: The analysis of leader cells trajectories revealed that VAPA KO leader cells were displacing faster but with a remarkable lack of directionality compared to Control leader cells (Figure 1F and G)
evidence: Supported by trajectory analysis data shown in Figure 1F and G

claim: Single VAPA KO cells displacing on a 2D surface exhibited identical defects compared to VAPA KO leader cells in monolayers.
source: This collective migration impairment was at least partially cell-intrinsic, as single VAPA KO cells displacing on a 2D surface exhibited identical defects compared to VAPA KO leader cells in monolayers (Figure 1H–J).
evidence: Supported by single cell migration data shown in Figure 1H-J

claim: VAPA KO cells were spreading much faster than Control cells upon plating.
source: Moreover, upon plating, VAPA KO cells were spreading much faster than Control cells, also indicating a cell-autonomous defect arising in these cells (Figure 1K and L).
evidence: Supported by cell spreading assay data shown in Figure 1K and L

claim: The expression of mCherry-VAPA WT restored either partially or totally the collective migration capacity of VAPA KO cells.
source: The expression of mCherry-VAPA WT restored either partially or totally the collective migration capacity of VAPA KO cells (Figure 1D–G and Video 1)
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 1D-G

claim: The VAPA KDMD mutant failed to rescue the collective migration phenotypes in VAPA KO cells.
source: Importantly, the VAPA KDMD mutant failed to rescue these phenotypes in VAPA KO cells (Figure 1D–G , and K–L and Video 1).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data with MSP mutant shown in Figure 1D-G and K-L

claim: VAPA is a novel actor of collective and individual cell motility processes.
source: Altogether, our results identify VAPA as a novel actor of collective and individual cell motility processes
evidence: Inferred from the collective migration and single cell migration defects observed in VAPA KO cells

claim: The FFAT-binding MSP domain plays a determinant role in VAPA protein function during cell motility.
source: Altogether, our results identify VAPA as a novel actor of collective and individual cell motility processes, and point to a determinant role of the FFAT-binding MSP domain in VAPA protein.
evidence: Inferred from the failure of VAPA KDMD mutant to rescue motility phenotypes

claim: VAPA KO cells formed larger central FA compared to Control cells.
source: We observed an alteration of cell-matrix adhesions in VAPA KO cells that formed larger central FA compared to Control cells (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by focal adhesion size quantification shown in Figure 2A and B

claim: Peripheral FA exhibited the same size in Control and VAPA KO cells.
source: Peripheral FA, located at the leading edge tip where nascent adhesions form, exhibited the same size in Control and VAPA KO cells (Figure 2A and C).
evidence: Supported by peripheral focal adhesion size quantification shown in Figure 2A and C

claim: The expression of VAPA WT in VAPA KO cells restored the size of central FA, but VAPA KDMD did not.
source: The expression of VAPA WT in VAPA KO cells restored the size of central FA, but it was not the case with VAPA KDMD, indicating that VAPA regulates FA size through its association with proteins containing an FFAT motif (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 2A-C

claim: VAPA regulates FA size through its association with proteins containing an FFAT motif.
source: The expression of VAPA WT in VAPA KO cells restored the size of central FA, but it was not the case with VAPA KDMD, indicating that VAPA regulates FA size through its association with proteins containing an FFAT motif (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Inferred from the failure of VAPA KDMD mutant to rescue FA size phenotype

claim: Control cells exhibit numerous and thick parallel transverse actin arcs at the front.
source: In Control cells, the F-actin and cortactin stainings revealed the presence of numerous and thick parallel transverse actin arcs at the front, accompanied by cortactin-rich subdomains of branched actin standing at the front edge corresponding to lamellipodial extensions (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: Supported by F-actin and cortactin staining shown in Figure 2D and E

claim: Control cells exhibit periodic waves of protrusion-retraction arising every 15 min in average.
source: We indeed observed periodic waves of protrusion-retraction arising in these cells every 15 min in average (Figure 2E and H).
evidence: Supported by kymograph analysis shown in Figure 2E and H

claim: VAPA KO cells exhibited disorganized and thinner transverse actin arcs.
source: By contrast, VAPA KO cells exhibited disorganized and thinner transverse actin arcs, wider cortactin-rich subdomains occupying most of the leading edge (Figure 2D and F–G)
evidence: Supported by F-actin and cortactin staining shown in Figure 2D and F-G

claim: VAPA KO cells exhibit wider cortactin-rich subdomains occupying most of the leading edge.
source: By contrast, VAPA KO cells exhibited disorganized and thinner transverse actin arcs, wider cortactin-rich subdomains occupying most of the leading edge (Figure 2D and F–G)
evidence: Supported by cortactin staining and quantification shown in Figure 2D and F-G

claim: VAPA KO cells give rise to long-lasting protrusions.
source: By contrast, VAPA KO cells exhibited disorganized and thinner transverse actin arcs, wider cortactin-rich subdomains occupying most of the leading edge (Figure 2D and F–G) and giving rise to long-lasting protrusions (Figure 2E and H).
evidence: Supported by kymograph analysis shown in Figure 2E and H

claim: VAPA controls the maintenance of FA size and the preservation of the spatial and temporal organization of the actin cytoskeleton.
source: To conclude, we show that VAPA controls different aspects of cell motility, namely the maintenance of FA size and the preservation of the spatial and temporal organization of the actin cytoskeleton.
evidence: Inferred from the FA size and actin organization defects observed in VAPA KO cells

claim: VAPA functions in FA size and actin organization depend on the association of VAPA with FFAT-motif containing proteins.
source: These functions depend on the association of VAPA with FFAT-motif containing proteins such as lipid transfer proteins, suggesting that lipid transfer is probably required.
evidence: Inferred from the failure of VAPA KDMD mutant to rescue phenotypes

claim: The depletion of VAPA alone was not sufficient to observe an accumulation of PI(4)P in early endosomes.
source: Importantly, the depletion of VAPA alone was not sufficient to observe an accumulation of PI(4)P in early endosomes (Figure 3B and C) which is in agreement with the SupFig. S1D by Dong et al., 2016 showing no effect on intra-cellular PI(4)P distribution when only VAPA is depleted in HeLa cells.
evidence: Supported by GFP-PH-OSBP probe data shown in Figure 3B and C, and consistent with published data from Dong et al., 2016

claim: VAPB can compensate for the absence of VAPA at ER-Golgi and ER-endosome contact sites thus maintaining PI(4)P homeostasis at the Golgi and endosomes in VAPA KO Caco-2 cells.
source: This result suggests that VAPB, which is slightly more abondant in VAPA KO cells, can compensate for the absence of VAPA at ER-Golgi and ER-endosome contact sites thus maintaining PI(4)P homeostasis at the Golgi and endosomes in VAPA KO Caco-2 cells.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of PI(4)P accumulation in Golgi and endosomes despite VAPA depletion

claim: The depletion of VAPA induced a decrease of the PM/cytosol ratio for both PI(4)P and PI(4,5)P2 in protrusive sub-domains of the leading edge.
source: The depletion of VAPA induced a decrease of the PM/cytosol ratio for both PI(4)P and PI(4,5)P2 in protrusive sub-domains of the leading edge (Figure 3D, E, H and I).
evidence: Supported by mCherry-P4M SidM and RFP-PH-PLCδ1 probe data shown in Figure 3D, E, H and I

claim: The decrease of PI(4,5)P2 in VAPA KO cells was also observed at the dorsal side of the PM by immunofluorescence staining with anti-PI(4,5)P2 antibodies.
source: The decrease of PI(4,5)P2 in VAPA KO cells was also observed at the dorsal side of the PM by immunofluorescence staining with anti-PI(4,5)P2 antibodies (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: Supported by anti-PI(4,5)P2 immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3F and G

claim: In Caco-2 cells, VAPA is required to maintain a certain level of PI(4)P and PI(4,5)P2 specifically at the plasma membrane.
source: Altogether, these results show that in Caco-2 cells, VAPA is required to maintain a certain level of PI(4)P and PI(4,5)P2 specifically at the plasma membrane
evidence: Inferred from the decreased PI(4)P and PI(4,5)P2 levels at the PM in VAPA KO cells

claim: VAPA is dispensable for PI(4)P homeostasis at the Golgi and endosomal compartments.
source: Altogether, these results show that in Caco-2 cells, VAPA is required to maintain a certain level of PI(4)P and PI(4,5)P2 specifically at the plasma membrane, but is dispensable for PI(4)P homeostasis at the Golgi and endosomal compartments.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of PI(4)P changes at Golgi and endosomes in VAPA KO cells

claim: GFP-MAPPER selectively labels ER-PM contact sites.
source: To this aim, we took advantage of a fluorescent probe, GFP-MAPPER, which selectively labels ER-PM contact sites (Chang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chang et al., 2013

claim: GFP-MAPPER distributed as foci along ER tubules both in Control and VAPA KO cells.
source: When expressed in Caco-2 cells, GFP-MAPPER distributed as foci along ER tubules both in Control and VAPA KO cells (Figure 4A)
evidence: Supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 4A

claim: GFP-MAPPER appeared at ER-PM appositions detected by TIRF microscopy.
source: When expressed in Caco-2 cells, GFP-MAPPER distributed as foci along ER tubules both in Control and VAPA KO cells (Figure 4A) and appeared at ER-PM appositions detected by TIRF microscopy (Figure 4B and Video 2).
evidence: Supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 4B

claim: GFP-MAPPER foci are found along VAPA-containing ER tubules.
source: Moreover, we could observe GFP-MAPPER foci along VAPA-containing ER tubules highlighted with an exogenous mCherry-VAPA WT protein expressed in Control cells (Figure 4C) or with an anti-VAPA antibody (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: At the front of leader cells, GFP-MAPPER foci divided in two subpools: the dorsal subpool ongoing forward movement with the migrating cell and the ventral subpool remaining immobile relative to the substrate.
source: At the front of leader cells, GFP-MAPPER foci divided in two subpools: the dorsal subpool ongoing forward movement with the migrating cell and the ventral subpool remaining immobile relative to the substrate, suggesting that ventral ER-PM contact sites might be anchored to cell-matrix adhesions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and Video 3).
evidence: Supported by spinning disk microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: Ventral ER-PM contact sites might be anchored to cell-matrix adhesions.
source: At the front of leader cells, GFP-MAPPER foci divided in two subpools: the dorsal subpool ongoing forward movement with the migrating cell and the ventral subpool remaining immobile relative to the substrate, suggesting that ventral ER-PM contact sites might be anchored to cell-matrix adhesions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and Video 3).
evidence: Inferred from the immobility of ventral GFP-MAPPER foci relative to the substrate

claim: Numerous ER-PM contact sites sit at the ventral leading edge of migrating cells.
source: Using electron microscopy, we were indeed able to identify numerous ER-PM contact sites sitting at the ventral leading edge of migrating cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4D

claim: At the ultrastructural level, the depletion of VAPA had no significant effect on ER-PM contact sites regardless of their location.
source: At the ultrastructural level, the depletion of VAPA had no significant effect on ER-PM contact sites regardless of their location (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-E

claim: Ventral ER-PM contact sites barely moved (400 nm/min on average) and persisted generally more than 10 min in Control cells.
source: However, the dynamic analysis of GFP-MAPPER foci revealed that ventral ER-PM contact sites, which barely moved (400 nm/min on average) and persisted generally more than 10 min in Control cells, were significantly less stable both spatially and temporally in VAPA KO cells (Figure 4E–G and Video 4).
evidence: Supported by GFP-MAPPER foci tracking data shown in Figure 4E-G

claim: Ventral ER-PM contact sites were significantly less stable both spatially and temporally in VAPA KO cells.
source: However, the dynamic analysis of GFP-MAPPER foci revealed that ventral ER-PM contact sites, which barely moved (400 nm/min on average) and persisted generally more than 10 min in Control cells, were significantly less stable both spatially and temporally in VAPA KO cells (Figure 4E–G and Video 4).
evidence: Supported by GFP-MAPPER foci tracking data showing increased speed and decreased lifetime in VAPA KO cells shown in Figure 4E-G

claim: There is a sub-pool of ER-PM contact sites docked to the substrate at the front of migrating cells, whose spatio-temporal stability requires VAPA.
source: To conclude, our results identify a sub-pool of ER-PM contact sites docked to the substrate at the front of migrating cells, and whose spatio-temporal stability requires VAPA.
evidence: Inferred from the decreased stability of ventral ER-PM contact sites in VAPA KO cells

claim: The assembly rate of FA was similar in both Control and VAPA KO cells.
source: While the assembly rate of FA was similar in both cell lines, their disassembly rate was slower in VAPA KO cells (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: Supported by FA dynamics analysis shown in Figure 5A-C

claim: The disassembly rate of FA was slower in VAPA KO cells.
source: While the assembly rate of FA was similar in both cell lines, their disassembly rate was slower in VAPA KO cells (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: Supported by FA dynamics analysis shown in Figure 5A-C

claim: VAPA KO FA exhibited a longer lifetime in average, with a majority lasting at least 40 min, instead of 30 min in Control cells.
source: In addition, VAPA KO FA exhibited a longer lifetime in average, with a majority lasting at least 40 min, instead of 30 min in Control cells (Figure 5A and D).
evidence: Supported by FA lifetime distribution analysis shown in Figure 5A and D

claim: The expression of VAPA WT in VAPA KO cells restored the lifetime of FA, unlike VAPA KDMD mutant.
source: The expression of VAPA WT in VAPA KO cells restored the lifetime of FA, unlike VAPA KDMD mutant, indicating that not only the size of FA but also their lifetime depended on the interaction of VAPA with FFAT-containing proteins (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 5D

claim: Not only the size of FA but also their lifetime depended on the interaction of VAPA with FFAT-containing proteins.
source: The expression of VAPA WT in VAPA KO cells restored the lifetime of FA, unlike VAPA KDMD mutant, indicating that not only the size of FA but also their lifetime depended on the interaction of VAPA with FFAT-containing proteins (Figure 5D).
evidence: Inferred from the failure of VAPA KDMD mutant to rescue FA lifetime phenotype

claim: Clathrin-mediated endocytosis of integrins has been shown to depend on microtubules.
source: One way to disassemble FA is through clathrin-mediated endocytosis of integrins which has been shown to depend on microtubules (Ezratty et al., 2009; Ezratty et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ezratty et al., 2009 and Ezratty et al., 2005

claim: In Control cells, nocodazole wash-out induced the fast recovery of the microtubule network after 15 min.
source: In Control cells, nocodazole wash-out induced the fast recovery of the microtubule network after 15 min (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by tubulin immunostaining shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A

claim: In Control cells, microtubule recovery was concomitant to the disassembly of FA attested by a 50% reduction of FA size.
source: In Control cells, nocodazole wash-out induced the fast recovery of the microtubule network after 15 min (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) concomitantly to the disassembly of FA attested by a 50% reduction of FA size.
evidence: Inferred from the temporal correlation between microtubule recovery and FA size reduction

claim: In VAPA KO cells, FA failed to disassemble upon microtubule recovery.
source: However, in VAPA KO cells, FA failed to disassemble upon microtubule recovery (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: Supported by nocodazole wash-out experiment data shown in Figure 5E and F

claim: VAPA is required for microtubule-dependent FA disassembly during migration of Caco2 cells.
source: These results demonstrate that VAPA is required for microtubule-dependent FA disassembly during migration of Caco2 cells.
evidence: Inferred from the failure of FA to disassemble upon microtubule recovery in VAPA KO cells

claim: In Control cells, the majority of central FA (75%) exhibited one or more GFP-MAPPER foci in their vicinity.
source: In Control cells, the majority of central FA (75%) exhibited one or more GFP-MAPPER foci in their vicinity (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: Supported by TIRF microscopy quantification shown in Figure 6A and B

claim: The peaks of the most proximal GFP-MAPPER foci partially superposed on the peaks of FA, with a distance of around 50–150 nm at 50% of the peaks.
source: Using super-resolutive Structured Illumination Microscopy (SIM), we could determine that the peaks of the most proximal GFP-MAPPER foci partially superposed on the peaks of FA, with a distance of around 50–150 nm at 50% of the peaks, suggesting that the two elements were either in contact or in close proximity.
evidence: Supported by SIM data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A

claim: GFP-MAPPER foci and FA are either in contact or in close proximity.
source: Using super-resolutive Structured Illumination Microscopy (SIM), we could determine that the peaks of the most proximal GFP-MAPPER foci partially superposed on the peaks of FA, with a distance of around 50–150 nm at 50% of the peaks, suggesting that the two elements were either in contact or in close proximity.
evidence: Inferred from the 50-150 nm distance measured by SIM

claim: Some GFP-MAPPER foci were found inside the perimeter of FA.
source: Some GFP-MAPPER foci were even found inside the perimeter of FA (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by SIM data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A

claim: In VAPA KO cells, only 30% of central FA were standing proximal to at least one GFP-MAPPER foci.
source: In VAPA KO cells, only 30% of central FA were standing proximal to at least one GFP-MAPPER foci (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: Supported by TIRF microscopy quantification shown in Figure 6A and B

claim: The expression of VAPA WT or the mutant VAPA KDMD in VAPA KO cells restored the high percentage of central FA proximal to GFP-MAPPER foci.
source: The expression of VAPA WT or the mutant VAPA KDMD in VAPA KO cells restored the high percentage of central FA proximal to GFP-MAPPER foci (Figure 6B), indicating that the MSP domain of VAPA was not required for the physical proximity between central FA and ER-PM contact sites.
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 6B

claim: The MSP domain of VAPA was not required for the physical proximity between central FA and ER-PM contact sites.
source: The expression of VAPA WT or the mutant VAPA KDMD in VAPA KO cells restored the high percentage of central FA proximal to GFP-MAPPER foci (Figure 6B), indicating that the MSP domain of VAPA was not required for the physical proximity between central FA and ER-PM contact sites.
evidence: Inferred from the ability of VAPA KDMD mutant to rescue the proximity phenotype

claim: Almost none of the peripheral FA were proximal to GFP-MAPPER foci.
source: Unlike central FA, almost none of the peripheral FA were proximal to GFP-MAPPER foci (Figure 6B), suggesting that ER-PM contact sites are probably getting closer to FA after their assembly.
evidence: Supported by TIRF microscopy quantification shown in Figure 6B

claim: ER-PM contact sites are probably getting closer to FA after their assembly.
source: Unlike central FA, almost none of the peripheral FA were proximal to GFP-MAPPER foci (Figure 6B), suggesting that ER-PM contact sites are probably getting closer to FA after their assembly.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of GFP-MAPPER foci near peripheral FA

claim: In Control cells, for most FA (71.4%), the first GFP-MAPPER foci appearing in the FA vicinity was detected after FA assembly and before its disassembly.
source: Indeed, when we monitored the time course of mCherry-Vinculin and GFP-MAPPER signals within the perimeter of single FA by TIRF microscopy, we could establish that in Control cells, for most FA (71,4%), the first GFP-MAPPER foci appearing in the FA vicinity was detected after FA assembly and before its disassembly, with a preferential arrival within the 10 min preceding disassembly (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse TIRF microscopy analysis shown in Figure 6C-E

claim: In Control cells, the first GFP-MAPPER foci has a preferential arrival within the 10 min preceding FA disassembly.
source: Indeed, when we monitored the time course of mCherry-Vinculin and GFP-MAPPER signals within the perimeter of single FA by TIRF microscopy, we could establish that in Control cells, for most FA (71,4%), the first GFP-MAPPER foci appearing in the FA vicinity was detected after FA assembly and before its disassembly, with a preferential arrival within the 10 min preceding disassembly (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse TIRF microscopy analysis shown in Figure 6C-E

claim: Once detected, the first GFP-MAPPER foci seemed to anchor to the pre-existing FA, as it was persisting 6 min on average in the FA vicinity in Control cells.
source: Once detected, this first GFP-MAPPER foci seemed to anchor to the pre-existing FA, as it was persisting 6 min on average in the FA vicinity (Figure 6C and F).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse TIRF microscopy analysis shown in Figure 6C and F

claim: In VAPA KO cells, there was no preferential time distribution of arrival of the first GFP-MAPPER foci, with 47.6% of them arriving before FA disassembly and 52.4% after FA disassembly.
source: In VAPA KO cells, where only 30% of FA were found in proximity to GFP-MAPPER foci (Figure 6A–B), there was no preferential time distribution of arrival of the first GFP-MAPPER foci, with 47,6% of them arriving before FA disassembly and 52.4% after FA disassembly (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse TIRF microscopy analysis shown in Figure 6C-E

claim: In VAPA KO cells, once detected, GFP-MAPPER foci were rapidly moving away from FA.
source: Once detected, these foci were rapidly moving away (Figure 6C and F).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse TIRF microscopy analysis shown in Figure 6C and F

claim: VAPA is required for the stable anchoring of ER-PM contact sites to pre-existing FA before and at the time of FA disassembly.
source: These results show that VAPA is required for the stable anchoring of ER-PM contact sites to pre-existing FA before and at the time of FA disassembly.
evidence: Inferred from the decreased stability and altered timing of GFP-MAPPER foci at FA in VAPA KO cells

claim: VAPA is present at GFP-MAPPER foci proximal to FA.
source: Imporantly, we were able to detect by TIRF microscopy the presence of VAPA at GFP-MAPPER foci proximal to FA (Figure 6G and H) reinforcing the idea that VAPA is indeed playing a role there.
evidence: Supported by TIRF microscopy data showing colocalization shown in Figure 6G and H

claim: The function of VAPA in cell migration seems to arise from its specific role at ER-PM contact sites where it was necessary to maintain high levels of PI(4)P and PI(4,5)P2 independently of VAPB.
source: The function of VAPA in cell migration seems to arise from its specific role at ER-PM contact sites where it was necessary to maintain high levels of PI(4)P and PI(4,5)P2 independently of VAPB.
evidence: Inferred from the specific decrease of PI(4)P and PI(4,5)P2 at the PM but not at Golgi/endosomes in VAPA KO cells

claim: Migration defects in VAPA KO cells were not a result of a dysfunction of lipid transfer in the secretory pathway.
source: This suggests that VAPB might compensate for the absence of VAPA at ER-Golgi and ER-endosomes contact sites and that migration defects in VAPA KO cells were not a result of a dysfunction of lipid transfer in the secretory pathway.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of PI(4)P changes at Golgi and endosomes in VAPA KO cells

claim: VAPA and VAPB might fulfill both redundant and specific tasks in lipid homeostasis and cellular functions.
source: Together with previous studies (Dong et al., 2016; Mao et al., 2019; Peretti et al., 2008; Stefan et al., 2011), our results converge to the idea that VAPA and VAPB might fulfill both redundant and specific tasks in lipid homeostasis and cellular functions.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of VAPA depletion at different cellular locations and supported by citations

claim: PI(4,5)P2 and its phosphorylation product PI(3,4,5)P3 have been described for decades as central orchestrators of cell motility through regulation of actin dynamics, FA maturation and turnover, membrane organization and curvature, and intracellular trafficking.
source: PI(4,5)P2 and its phosphorylation product PI(3,4,5)P3 have been described for decades as central orchestrators of cell motility through regulation of actin dynamics, FA maturation and turnover, membrane organization and curvature, and intracellular trafficking (Mandal, 2020; Tsujita and Itoh, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mandal, 2020 and Tsujita and Itoh, 2015

claim: Altering the global synthesis of PI(4,5)P2 results in defects that are comparable to the ones observed in VAPA KO cells – namely disorganization of actin, protrusion defects, FA persistence and loss of directional movement.
source: Notably, several previous studies have shown that altering the global synthesis of PI(4,5)P2, either by knockdown of certain isoforms of the PIPKI kinase which phosphorylates PI(4)P (Chao et al., 2010a, Chao et al., 2010b; Thapa et al., 2012), or by optogenetic approaches (Idevall-Hagren et al., 2012; Xiong et al., 2016), results in defects that are comparable to the ones observed in VAPA KO cells – namely disorganization of actin, protrusion defects, FA persistence and loss of directional movement.
evidence: Supported by citations to Chao et al., 2010a, Chao et al., 2010b, Thapa et al., 2012, Idevall-Hagren et al., 2012, and Xiong et al., 2016

claim: The phenotypes of VAPA KO cells could be solely explained by a global reduction in PI(4,5)P2 levels at the PM.
source: Thus, the phenotypes of VAPA KO cells could be solely explained by a global reduction in PI(4,5)P2 levels at the PM.
evidence: Inferred from the similarity between VAPA KO phenotypes and phenotypes caused by PI(4,5)P2 reduction

claim: VAPA not only regulates PI(4,5)P2 homeostasis at the PM, but also fulfills a function at FA where it stably anchors ER-PM contact sites and promotes microtubule-dependent FA disassembly.
source: However, our results clearly show that VAPA not only regulates PI(4,5)P2 homeostasis at the PM, but also fulfills a function at FA where it stably anchors ER-PM contact sites and promotes microtubule-dependent FA disassembly.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations of PI(4,5)P2 regulation, ER-PM contact site anchoring, and FA disassembly defects

claim: This work provides for the first time a quantitative spatio-temporal connection between ER-PM contact sites and FA dynamics in polarized and migrating cells.
source: Importantly, we provide for the first time a quantitative spatio-temporal connection between ER-PM contact sites and FA dynamics in polarized and migrating cells.
evidence: Based on the novel quantitative analysis of GFP-MAPPER foci dynamics relative to FA

claim: VAPA, through local regulation of lipid transfer in the vicinity of FA would induce the internalization of integrins through clathrin-mediated endocytosis which depends on PI(4,5)P2 levels and on microtubule polymerization.
source: Based on these results, we propose a hypothetical model in which VAPA, through local regulation of lipid transfer in the vicinity of FA would induce the internalization of integrins through clathrin-mediated endocytosis which depends on PI(4,5)P2 levels (Chao et al., 2010a, Chao et al., 2010b; Nader et al., 2016) and on microtubule polymerization (Ezratty et al., 2009).
evidence: Speculative model based on the observed data and supported by citations to Chao et al., 2010a, Chao et al., 2010b, Nader et al., 2016, and Ezratty et al., 2009

claim: MCS have been shown to directly regulate endocytosis in yeast.
source: Interestingly, MCS have already been shown to directly regulate endocytosis in yeast (Encinar Del Dedo et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Encinar Del Dedo et al., 2017

claim: The MSP domain of VAPA is required for the regulation of FA dynamics.
source: Through which mechanisms could VAPA control the dynamics of FA and their close proximity with ER-PM contact sites? Our results show that the MSP domain of VAPA is required for the regulation of FA dynamics.
evidence: Inferred from the failure of VAPA KDMD mutant to rescue FA dynamics phenotypes

claim: Nir2 and ORP3 are potential drivers for the specific function of VAPA at FA.
source: Importantly, two lipid transfer proteins interacting with VAPA at ER-PM contact sites, Nir2 and ORP3, have been previously described as regulators of FA dynamics and cell motility, establishing them as potential drivers for the specific function of VAPA at FA.
evidence: Inferred from the known interactions of Nir2 and ORP3 with VAPA and their roles in FA dynamics

claim: Nir2 interacts with VAPs at ER-PM and ER-Golgi contact sites and regulates PI transport.
source: Nir2, which interacts with VAPs at ER-PM and ER-Golgi contact sites and regulates PI transport (Chang and Liou, 2015; Kim et al., 2013; Peretti et al., 2008), favors epithelial-mesenchymal transition and tumor metastasis (Keinan et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chang and Liou, 2015, Kim et al., 2013, Peretti et al., 2008, and Keinan et al., 2014

claim: The depletion of Nir2 in HeLa cells induces a decrease of PI(4,5)P2 levels at the PM.
source: Similarly to VAPA KO cells, the depletion of Nir2 in HeLa cells induces a decrease of PI(4,5)P2 levels at the PM (Kim et al., 2013), indicating that a part of VAPA effect on PInst homeostasis could be supported by VAPA/Nir2-mediated lipid transfer.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim et al., 2013

claim: A part of VAPA effect on PInst homeostasis could be supported by VAPA/Nir2-mediated lipid transfer.
source: Similarly to VAPA KO cells, the depletion of Nir2 in HeLa cells induces a decrease of PI(4,5)P2 levels at the PM (Kim et al., 2013), indicating that a part of VAPA effect on PInst homeostasis could be supported by VAPA/Nir2-mediated lipid transfer.
evidence: Inferred from the similarity between VAPA KO and Nir2 depletion phenotypes

claim: ORP3 extracts PI(4)P from the PM at ER-PM contact sites.
source: ORP3, which extracts PI(4)P from the PM at ER-PM contact sites (Gulyás et al., 2020), positively regulates the R-Ras pathway promoting cell-matrix adhesion (Lehto et al., 2008; Weber-Boyvat et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gulyás et al., 2020, Lehto et al., 2008, and Weber-Boyvat et al., 2015

claim: ORP3 was found to be recruited to disassembling FA upon calcium influx and to favour their turnover through lipid exchange and crosstalk with STIM1/Orai1-mediated calcium influx.
source: More recently, ORP3 was found to be recruited to disassembling FA upon calcium influx and to favour their turnover through lipid exchange and crosstalk with STIM1/Orai1-mediated calcium influx (D'Souza et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to D'Souza et al., 2020

claim: VAPA might also associate to FFAT-lacking proteins that would mediate the anchoring of ER to FA.
source: But VAPA might not act at FA just through its MSP domain. Indeed, we show that VAPA favours the proximity between FA and ER-PM contact sites independently of its MSP domain. Thus, we could imagine that VAPA also associates to FFAT-lacking proteins that would mediate the anchoring of ER to FA.
evidence: Inferred from the MSP-independent rescue of FA-ER-PM contact site proximity

claim: Kinectin has been shown to control the apposition of ER to FA through a microtubule-dependent transport.
source: Kinectin, an integral ER membrane protein interacting with kinesin, has been shown to control the apposition of ER to FA through a microtubule-dependent transport (Guadagno et al., 2020; Ng et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Guadagno et al., 2020 and Ng et al., 2016

claim: PTP1B localizes to the cytoplasmic face of the ER and was identified as a partner of VAPA using a BioID approach.
source: Another protein, the phosphatase PTP1B, which localizes to the cytoplasmic face of the ER and was identified as a partner of VAPA using a BioID approach (Antonicka et al., 2020), is targeted to newly formed FA and contributes to their maturation through dephosphorylation of its substrate p130Cas (Dadke and Chernoff, 2002; Hernández et al., 2006; Liu et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Antonicka et al., 2020, Dadke and Chernoff, 2002, Hernández et al., 2006, and Liu et al., 1998

claim: The role of VAPA-mediated contact sites at FA could be the establishment of a common platform mediating the anchoring of ER and microtubules close to FA where several processes, like lipid transfer, calcium exchange and vesicular transport could converge and participate to FA dynamics.
source: Therefore, the role of VAPA-mediated contact sites at FA could not only be the local modulation of lipid transfer, but also the establishment of a common platform mediating the anchoring of ER and microtubules close to FA where several processes, like lipid transfer, calcium exchange and vesicular transport could converge and participate to FA dynamics.
evidence: Speculative model based on the observed data and known functions of ER proteins at FA

claim: This study reveals unknown functions for VAPA in cell motility processes and in local anchoring of ER-PM contact sites to FA.
source: To conclude, our study reveals unknown functions for VAPA in cell motility processes and in local anchoring of ER-PM contact sites to FA.
evidence: Summary of the novel findings presented in the study

claim: Lipid transfer would be an additional pathway for lipids to be controlled at FA.
source: For a long time, we have assumed that PInst regulation at FA will principally be mediated by the interplay of lipid kinases and phosphatases. Our work reinforces the idea that lipid transfer would be an additional pathway for lipids to be controlled at FA
evidence: Inferred from the role of VAPA-mediated lipid transfer at FA

claim: This work provides evidences for a spatio-temporal connection between MCS and FA mediated by VAPA.
source: Our work reinforces the idea that lipid transfer would be an additional pathway for lipids to be controlled at FA and provides evidences for a spatio-temporal connection between MCS and FA mediated by VAPA.
evidence: Based on the quantitative analysis of ER-PM contact site dynamics relative to FA

claim: PI(4,5)P2 controls FA dynamics by regulating the binding of talin to integrins.
source: PI(4,5)P2, the most abundant PInst at the plasma membrane, controls FA dynamics by regulating the binding of talin to integrins (Martel et al., 2001; Thapa et al., 2012) and the polarized trafficking of integrins (Nader et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Martel et al., 2001 and Thapa et al., 2012

claim: PI(4,5)P2 controls the polarized trafficking of integrins.
source: PI(4,5)P2, the most abundant PInst at the plasma membrane, controls FA dynamics by regulating the binding of talin to integrins (Martel et al., 2001; Thapa et al., 2012) and the polarized trafficking of integrins (Nader et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nader et al., 2016

claim: PI(4,5)P2 is described as a modulator of actin cytoskeleton organization and dynamics, either directly through the recruitment of several actin-binding proteins, or indirectly by regulating the activation of RhoA and Cdc42 GTPases.
source: PI(4,5)P2 is described as a modulator of actin cytoskeleton organization and dynamics, either directly through the recruitment of several actin-binding proteins (Senju et al., 2017), or indirectly by regulating the activation of RhoA (Lacalle et al., 2007; Xu et al., 2010) and Cdc42 GTPases (Daste et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Senju et al., 2017, Lacalle et al., 2007, Xu et al., 2010, and Daste et al., 2017

claim: PI(3,4,5)P3 acts as a 'compass lipid' that stabilizes the direction of migration through the activation of Rac1.
source: Several in vitro and in vivo studies have shown that PI(3,4,5)P3 acts as a 'compass lipid' that stabilizes the direction of migration (Funamoto et al., 2002; Hannigan et al., 2002; Lam et al., 2012) through the activation of Rac1 (Kunisaki et al., 2006; Welch et al., 2002; Yoshii et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Funamoto et al., 2002, Hannigan et al., 2002, Lam et al., 2012, Kunisaki et al., 2006, Welch et al., 2002, and Yoshii et al., 1999

claim: MCS are sites of close apposition between two membranes, often the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane and the membrane of another organelle, at a distance of less than 80 nm, where exchanges of lipids, Ca2+ and metabolites take place.
source: MCS are sites of close apposition between two membranes, often the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane and the membrane of another organelle, at a distance of less than 80 nm, where exchanges of lipids, Ca2 +and metabolites take place (Prinz et al., 2020; Scorrano et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Prinz et al., 2020, Scorrano et al., 2019, and Wu et al., 2018

claim: The activity of lipid transfer at MCS was observed decades ago.
source: While the activity of lipid transfer at MCS was observed decades ago (Vance, 1990), their implication in patho-physiological processes such as cell motility has gained interest only recently (Prinz et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Vance, 1990 and Prinz et al., 2020

claim: VAPA is a member of the highly conserved VAP family of proteins, together with VAPB.
source: VAPA is a member of the highly conserved VAP family of proteins, together with VAPB.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about VAP protein family

claim: VAP proteins are integral ER membrane proteins bridging the ER membrane to the membrane of other compartments by assembling with numerous partners including lipid transfer proteins that bind the target membrane, such as Nir proteins and OSBP-related (ORP) proteins.
source: VAP proteins are integral ER membrane proteins bridging the ER membrane to the membrane of other compartments by assembling with numerous partners including lipid transfer proteins that bind the target membrane, such as Nir proteins and OSBP-related (ORP) proteins.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about VAP protein function

claim: The assembly of most of VAP complexes relies on the interaction between the conserved N-terminal MSP (Major Sperm Protein) domain of VAPs and the FFAT (2 phenyl alanines in an acidic tract) motif on their partner.
source: The assembly of most of VAP complexes relies on the interaction between the conserved N-terminal MSP (Major Sperm Protein) domain of VAPs and the FFAT (2 phenyl alanines in an acidic tract) motif on their partner.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about VAP protein interactions

claim: VAPs contain a central coiled-coil dimerization domain and an ER transmembrane domain in their C-terminus.
source: VAPs also contain a central coiled-coil dimerization domain and an ER transmembrane domain in their C-terminus (Murphy and Levine, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Murphy and Levine, 2016

claim: VAP proteins are involved in several cellular functions such as lipid transport, membrane trafficking, the unfolded protein response pathway and microtubules organization.
source: VAP proteins are involved in several cellular functions such as lipid transport, membrane trafficking, the unfolded protein response pathway and microtubules organization (Kamemura and Chihara, 2019; Lev et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kamemura and Chihara, 2019 and Lev et al., 2008

claim: At ER-PM contact sites, the VAP/Nir2 and VAP/ORP3 complexes regulate the transport of Phosphoinositol (PI) and PI(4)P respectively.
source: At ER-PM contact sites, the VAP/Nir2 and VAP/ORP3 complexes regulate the transport of Phosphoinositol (PI) and PI(4)P respectively.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about VAP complexes at ER-PM contact sites

claim: VAP complexes with membrane-associated kinases and phosphatases contribute to modulating locally the pool of PI(4)P, PI(4,5)P2 and PI(3,4,5)P3 at the PM.
source: Together with membrane-associated kinases and phosphatases, they contribute to modulating locally the pool of PI(4)P, PI(4,5)P2 and PI(3,4,5)P3 at the PM (Chang and Liou, 2015; Gulyás et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chang and Liou, 2015, Gulyás et al., 2020, and Kim et al., 2013

claim: The association of VAPs with OSBP-related proteins modifies the level of PI(4)P at endosomal membranes and at the Golgi, therefore regulating trafficking events in these two compartments.
source: In addition, the association of VAPs with OSBP-related proteins modifies the level of PI(4)P at endosomal membranes and at the Golgi, therefore regulating trafficking events in these two compartments (Dong et al., 2016; Kawasaki et al., 2022; Mesmin et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dong et al., 2016, Kawasaki et al., 2022, and Mesmin et al., 2013

claim: VAP proteins mediate cholesterol transport at ER-Golgi, ER-endosome and ER-peroxisome MCS.
source: Moreover, VAP proteins mediate cholesterol transport at ER-Golgi, ER-endosome and ER-peroxisome MCS (Dong et al., 2019; Hua et al., 2017; Mesmin et al., 2013; Wilhelm et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dong et al., 2019, Hua et al., 2017, Mesmin et al., 2013, and Wilhelm et al., 2017

claim: Depending on the cell type and organism, the loss of VAP proteins can lead to either a reduction or an accumulation of PI(4)P levels in the Golgi membranes and its redistribution on endosomes.
source: Depending on the cell type and organism, the loss of VAP proteins can lead to either a reduction (Peretti et al., 2008) or an accumulation (Mao et al., 2019; Wakana et al., 2021; Subra et al., 2023) of PI(4)P levels in the Golgi membranes and its redistribution on endosomes (Dong et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Peretti et al., 2008, Mao et al., 2019, Wakana et al., 2021, Subra et al., 2023, and Dong et al., 2016

claim: In yeast, depleting VAP orthologs results in the accumulation of PI(4)P at the plasma membrane.
source: In yeast, depleting VAP orthologs results in the accumulation of PI(4)P at the plasma membrane (Stefan et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stefan et al., 2011

claim: Two partners of VAPs at ER-PM contact sites, ORP3 and Nir2, have been shown to regulate cell motility processes through different pathways.
source: Importantly, two partners of VAPs at ER-PM contact sites, ORP3 and Nir2, have been shown to regulate cell motility processes through different pathways (D'Souza et al., 2020; Keinan et al., 2014; Lehto et al., 2008; Weber-Boyvat et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to D'Souza et al., 2020, Keinan et al., 2014, Lehto et al., 2008, and Weber-Boyvat et al., 2015

claim: VAPB is not sufficient to compensate for the loss of VAPA in cell motility.
source: We observed strong motility defects, suggesting that VAPA is required for proper cell motility and that VAPB is not sufficient to compensate for the loss of VAPA.
evidence: Inferred from the motility defects observed in VAPA KO cells despite the presence of VAPB

claim: VAPA regulates the dynamics of focal adhesions (FA) through its MSP domain.
source: Importantly, we show that VAPA regulates the dynamics of focal adhesions (FA) through its MSP domain
evidence: Inferred from the failure of VAPA KDMD mutant to rescue FA dynamics phenotypes

claim: VAPA is essential to stabilize and anchor ventral ER-PM contact sites to FA.
source: Importantly, we show that VAPA regulates the dynamics of focal adhesions (FA) through its MSP domain, is essential to stabilize and anchor ventral ER-PM contact sites to FA
evidence: Inferred from the decreased stability and altered anchoring of ER-PM contact sites to FA in VAPA KO cells

claim: VAPA mediates microtubule-dependent FA disassembly.
source: Importantly, we show that VAPA regulates the dynamics of focal adhesions (FA) through its MSP domain, is essential to stabilize and anchor ventral ER-PM contact sites to FA, and mediates microtubule-dependent FA disassembly.
evidence: Inferred from the failure of FA to disassemble upon microtubule recovery in VAPA KO cells

claim: The depletion of VAPA strongly impacts the organization of the actin cytoskeleton, the dynamics of protrusions and the turnover of FA during migration.
source: Here, we show that the depletion of VAPA strongly impacts the organization of the actin cytoskeleton, the dynamics of protrusions and the turnover of FA during migration.
evidence: Inferred from the actin disorganization, protrusion defects, and FA turnover defects observed in VAPA KO cells

claim: The role of VAPA stands mainly at the PM where it regulates PI(4)P and PI(4,5)P2 homeostasis.
source: The role of VAPA stands mainly at the PM where it regulates PI(4)P and PI(4,5)P2 homeostasis, the stability of ER-PM contact sites and their local anchoring at FA, thereby regulating FA disassembly.
evidence: Inferred from the specific decrease of PI(4)P and PI(4,5)P2 at the PM but not at other compartments in VAPA KO cells
